title: Privately Clipping Heavy-Tailed Data
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Our adaptive clipping method stays near the non-private optimum across datasets and budgets, while fixed-quantile and prior baselines vary widely.
layout: 10 small line plots, 5x2 grid, shared legend at bottom
description: A 5-row by 2-column grid of line plots, one per dataset: steam, reddit, lastfm, hn, movielens, pantry, twitch, foursquare, jester and slashdot. Each plot has the clipping privacy budget (rho_clip, 0.01 to 0.1) on the x-axis and error ratio versus the non-private optimum on the y-axis. Five methods appear as colored dotted or dashed lines with circular markers. OptimizeRC is a solid blue line. HLY-UQ is orange dashed. UQ at q=0.9 is green dash-dot, q=0.95 is red dotted, and q=0.99 is purple dash-dot. A single legend sits at the bottom. The blue line stays close to 1 in nearly every panel, while the baselines often sit far higher. Y-axis scales differ by panel, and the purple line reaches 40 on lastfm and about 140 on foursquare. Most lines are flat across the budget range.
caption: Plots of OptimizeRC’s performance against UQ (q = {0.9, 0.95, 0.99}) and HLY-UQ. Each line is a different method, and each point on the line represents the mean of 100 trials per ρclip ∈{0.01, 0.02, . . . , 0.1}. We plot ratios of the mean MSE with respect to the (non-private) MSE-optimal Optimal, so a lower value is better.
abstract: Summing vectors is a basic task in differentially private data analysis. Standard private sum algorithms clip vectors to some bound, sum them, and add noise scaled to the bound. The differential privacy literature has developed a deep library of noise addition mechanisms, but it offers few tools for privately choosing a clipping bound based on the data. We introduce a method that privately chooses a clipping bound by optimizing residual coherence, the directional alignment of vectors exceeding the bound, against the variance cost of additional noise. We prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a general class of heavy-tailed data regimes and show empirically that, across several datasets, our method outperforms existing baselines.
